Introduction

Overview of the semester

This workbook documents my learning, process, and reflection across three assessments in Intersensory Digital Publishing this semester. It is not a polished record of perfect practice. It is an honest account of a semester in which I engaged deeply with some things, and not nearly enough with others.

What I made this semester surprised me. I came in expecting to learn about accessible publishing as a technical compliance problem. What I left with was an understanding of access as a relational and creative practice — something that changes the work itself, not just the delivery mechanism.

The throughline across all three assessments turned out to be the same question in different registers: how do you translate embodied, sensory experience into a form that can reach people who experience the world differently from you? In A1, that was language describing movement. In A3, it was a layered physical and digital system built so that touch, hearing, proximity, and haptics could carry a story that didn't rely on sight alone.

I didn't attend class as consistently as I should have. I'm naming that directly because this workbook asks for honest self-assessment, and pretending otherwise would undermine the only criterion I can still control.

Assessment 1 — Audio Description

Water Motor · Trisha Brown (1978) · Filmmaker: Babette Mangolte

The Work

The task was to write an audio description of Trisha Brown's Water Motor, a 1978 solo performance filmed by Babette Mangolte. Audio description is the practice of making visual content accessible to blind and low vision audiences through narrated description. Water Motor is two and a half minutes of extraordinarily dense movement: a cascade of kicks, coils, weight shifts, suspensions, runs and dissolves that repeat once in real time and once in slow motion.

Research — Audio Description of Dance

I researched existing audio description of dance before making A1. I needed to understand the language practitioners use before I could develop my own.

Preferred — Narrative approach

Yuldea (2023) — The describer makes the dance sound like a story. I'm attracted to narrative by instinct, and finding it here made me realise audio description doesn't have to be neutral inventory. It can have a perspective.

Reconsidered — Restraint as method

Alvin Ailey: Chroma, Grace, Takademe, Revelations — My initial reaction was that the description wasn't keeping up. On reflection I think there are moments where the describer deliberately steps back and lets the violins carry the emotion. Restraint rather than presence — and I'm not sure it's wrong, just not how I would do it.

Both works answer the same question differently: when another sense is already doing the work, do you describe anyway, or do you get out of the way? I instinctively preferred presence over restraint. That preference shaped my dual-layer approach to Water Motor, and later, Annie's audio design.

Process

I chose Water Motor specifically because of all the video examples available, it had a structure I could partially recognise: dance. I have some dance background, and that gave me a foothold — I could identify some of what Trisha Brown was doing technically, and feel the expressiveness of her movement in a way that came from having been in a body trying to move similarly.

My initial approach — simply describing what I saw — was immediately inadequate. The choreography operates at a speed and density that defeats literal description. Something else was getting lost too: her movements are impressionistic as much as technical. They feel like something. Flattening that into a list of steps would be accurate and useless.

I developed two parallel layers. The first was a rhythmic, beat-driven technical layer — drawing on Laban Movement Analysis effort qualities (sustained vs. sudden, strong vs. light, direct vs. indirect, bound vs. free) and the counting technique from dance class, where a teacher counts moves to an eight beat. The second layer ran alongside it: the emotional and impressionistic layer, about what the movement felt like to watch. These two layers wove in and out of each other, with one always slightly dominant depending on what the choreography was doing.

Rather than fighting the speed of the dance, I let myself lightly keep up — not minding if I missed individual steps, because any listener would too. The goal was to capture her spirit, not produce a complete inventory.

The written transcript took this further. I formatted the two scripts on either side of the page, aligned so the text itself formed a wave-like pattern down the document. The shape of the writing on the page was designed to echo the rhythm and movement of the dance. The transcript wasn't just a record of the audio — it was its own intersensory object, using text as visual form to show what the work was doing temporally and kinetically.

'She's announcing what's coming before she commits to it. Each kick a draft of the one that follows. The movement rehearsing itself. Energy accumulating through repetition. The body making good on a promise it's been building.'

The Grade and What I Missed

I got a lower grade on A1 than I was expecting, and it genuinely upset me. The reason was straightforward: I misread the rubric and didn't submit the required 500-word written brief about the work. It was an easy thing to write. I just didn't know it was required.

This semester has been hard to navigate. I deal with ADHD and anxiety, and both were heavier than usual. My pattern was to read enough to do the work and engage in class when something landed — but I missed things that required sustained administrative attention. The brief was one of them.

What I'm taking from it: the work itself isn't enough if you don't demonstrate your understanding of it in the form the assessment asks for. I knew what I did. I just didn't write it down.

What I Learned

Audio description forced me to understand that language is always a translation, never a reproduction. The question isn't 'what did I see' but 'what does the listener need to feel the thing I saw.' That distinction — between accuracy and accessibility — turned out to be foundational to everything that followed.

The dual-layer structure was also the first time I understood intersensory publishing as a layering problem rather than a translation problem. You don't replace one sense with another. You build depth by running multiple registers simultaneously. That thinking went directly into Annie's project. I didn't fully register at the time that using text as wave-shaped visual form was intersensory thinking — looking back, it was the same instinct as Annie's haptic feedback design.

In trying to make something layered, there are parts where I compromised on the actual audio description — particularly in the slow-motion repeat. I made pacing choices based on what I as an audience member would find engaging rather than what a blind viewer might need. That's a tension I didn't fully resolve.

Assessment 2 — Pitch

'Excuse me, do you have a minute?' · Site-specific intersensory digital publication · Royal Botanic Gardens Melbourne

Making Without a Map

A2 felt vague to me while I was in it. We were still working through audio description in class, and I couldn't find much existing work that I felt genuinely pulled toward as a model for what I wanted to make. There was nothing shown in class that directly inspired this project. That left me with the readings and my own real-world experience as the primary material — which turned out to be the right constraint, even if it didn't feel that way at the time. The project that emerged is more personal and more theoretically grounded than it would have been if I'd had a clear visual precedent to work from or against.

The one exception was Fayen d'Evie, who I found through my own research. She was the closest existing precedent I could locate — and finding her outside of class was important. It meant I'd gone looking rather than waiting to be shown.

Where the Concept Came From

The pitch began somewhere completely different — an underground street race embedded in the Tan. The constraints dismantled it systematically. GPS is accurate to three to five metres on consumer devices — useless for a race where a metre matters. QR codes require you to stop and orient your camera, breaking running flow. Web NFC is blocked on iPhone without a native app. Visually impaired runners almost always run with a dedicated guide — so a solo QR race was exclusionary by design.

Every constraint said the same thing: slow down. The Botanic Gardens sits right beside the Tan. No running allowed. That turned out to be exactly right for what this was becoming.

The non-linear structure came from not wanting to prescribe a path through the gardens. Non-linear narrative pointed toward memory. Memory pointed toward Alzheimer's. Annie emerged from a structural decision I made before I knew who she was. Form generated the story.

Theoretical Framework — What I Actually Thought

The A2 pitch was grounded in disability justice frameworks. I want to be honest about how I actually engaged with each text rather than just listing them as influences.

Mia Mingus — Access Intimacy was the most generative and also the most uncomfortable. I understood it immediately — I've been in situations where you go from feeling weird and excluded to suddenly feeling seen and included, and I know how powerful that shift can be. The concept landed.

But I pushed back on it in the context of my own work. Access intimacy, when it works, is natural — it emerges from genuine relational practice, not from being engineered. I was deliberately constructing the conditions for a stranger to feel seen and accompanied by a character I invented. That risks being performative in exactly the way Mingus's concept resists. I used access intimacy as the model while being genuinely uncertain whether a designed experience can ever achieve what Mingus is describing, or whether it only ever approximates it.

Carmen Papalia I found less challenging. His work — using a twenty-foot white cane on busy streets to create antagonism, leading sighted people on walks with their eyes closed — is directly adjacent to Annie: designed encounters in public space that make access felt rather than just provided. His manifesto was useful as validation for treating every design decision as a creative act, not just a technical one. But I'd already made those decisions before I read him. He confirmed rather than shifted.

Hamraie was genuinely unsettling. The critique of universal design — that designing for everyone can mean designing for no one — hit directly against something I was doing. The iOS/Android tension is a live example. Blind and low vision users overwhelmingly prefer iOS. VoiceOver is trusted and deeply integrated. But Web NFC is blocked on iOS entirely. I couldn't resolve it. I named it instead.

Fayen d'Evie and Benjamin Hancock's vibrational poetics practice I found through my own research rather than the assigned reading list. It was the closest existing precedent to what Annie was trying to be — site-specific, multisensory, Australian. Finding it mattered because it meant the concept wasn't unprecedented. Someone serious had already done adjacent work.

Mills and Sanchez on crip authorship raised the question I put to the class in the pitch: who gets to author work about disability? I'm making a work about Alzheimer's from outside that experience. My connection is personal — my grandmother — but personal isn't the same as lived. I don't think that question has a clean resolution.

What I Learned

I learned to let constraints do creative work rather than treating them as problems to solve. The race became Annie not despite the constraints but because of them. I also learned that naming unresolved questions is more honest and ultimately more interesting than pretending to have answers.

Assessment 3 — Build

'Excuse me, do you have a minute?' · PWA · Royal Botanic Gardens Melbourne

What Was Built

A Progressive Web App (PWA) in vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with GPS geofencing, local storage for first-visit detection, a garden map showing checkpoint proximity, and Web Vibration API haptic feedback throughout. The mapping stack was rebuilt from Mapbox to Leaflet with OpenStreetMap after a GitHub token exposure incident forced an immediate revocation of the Mapbox API key.

The map itself was designed as more than wayfinding. I overlaid an SVG layer on the Leaflet tile map and applied a stack of CSS/SVG filters — blur, contrast, hue-rotation, and opacity — to make the map read as a fuzzy memory rather than a precise navigational tool. The visual effect was intentional: Annie's experience of the garden is not cartographic. It is felt and half-remembered. The distorted map reflects that.

Audio for Stop 2 (The Gazebo). A custom NFC checkpoint puck — 3D modelled and printed — designed to house a QR code, NFC tag, Bluetooth beacon, and tactile dot border in a weatherproof disc.

Sylvia

The audio for Stop 2 was performed by Sylvia, my neighbour. I reached out to my immediate community rather than trying to cast a stranger — partly because I knew Sylvia's voice had exactly the quality Annie needed: warm, unhurried, the kind of voice that has lived in it. In exchange for her time I helped her move things around her home, since she is older and it's not always easy to manage alone.

I knew she'd be good. I didn't expect her to be as good as she was. She actually tried. She brought herself to it fully — she wasn't just reading lines, she was being Annie. That surprised me, and it made the recording something I couldn't have made alone.

Stop 2 — The Gazebo

QR Trigger · Voice: Sylvia · MP3

Annie at the second checkpoint — the gazebo, connected to a specific memory of Ron. This is what access intimacy sounds like when it isn't designed for.

Looking back, this is the closest the project came to what Mingus means by access intimacy — not something I designed for, but something that emerged from asking someone real, in my actual community, for something real. I'd been skeptical that you could engineer access intimacy without it becoming performative. With Sylvia it just happened. The work created the conditions and the relationship did the rest.

The Comment in Class

When I presented the pitch in A2, another student said: 'that's a lot of work, I don't think it's realistic — that would take a team.'

It terrified me. Because I'd been thinking exactly the same thing privately. I'd been telling myself it was manageable and someone had just said out loud what I was afraid was true.

I built most of it anyway. Alone. In a semester that was already hard. The animation didn't get finished and the site test didn't happen. But the puck exists. The audio exists. The PWA exists. The theoretical framework is solid. For one person, in one semester, with everything else going on, that's not nothing.

What I'm Most Proud Of

This was my most technically challenging project of the semester and probably of my degree so far. But the technical complexity isn't what I'm proudest of.

What I'm proudest of is that the work is intersensory at every level — not just in its design, but in its subject matter. Annie has Alzheimer's. Her experience of memory is fragmentary, non-linear, dependent on what she happens to stumble into. The PWA mirrors that structure exactly: no prescribed path, checkpoints encountered by chance, story experienced in whatever order the participant finds them. The form enacts the condition it's about. That's not something I planned from the start — it emerged from following the constraints.

Design vs. Fabrication — NFC Checkpoint Puck

The puck was specified in the A2 pitch as a 100mm circular object housing a QR code, NFC tag, Bluetooth beacon, tactile dot border, and weatherproof ABS casing. Below: specification diagram, 3D model render, and printed prototype.

Specified Design — Pitch Deck
3D Model — STL Render
Printed Prototype — Top View
Printed Prototype — Side Profile

The housing is yellow rather than neutral grey — yellow on white performs well for low vision users in variable outdoor light, which was in the original accessibility brief. The tactile dot border is present and legible by touch. The depth is shallower than the 22mm spec: the Bluetooth beacon didn't arrive in time due to a shipping issue, so there was nothing to house. Printing to full depth with no component to fill it would have added significant print time for no functional reason. The depth was reduced accordingly. This is a prototyping decision — the next version would be printed to full spec once the beacon hardware is in hand. The QR sticker is applied and functional, though slightly off-centre.

Self-Assessment

I didn't finish it. And I didn't test what I did finish. That's a failure of follow-through I can't dress up as anything else.

Part of this was bandwidth. Part of it was the ADHD tax on sustained execution of complex multi-component projects. The beacon not arriving was a real logistical problem — but if I'm honest, it also became an easier reason not to push forward with what I could have tested without it. The site test required going to the gardens and confronting whether the thing I'd designed actually worked in physical space. That's the scariest part of any site-specific project. I didn't do it.

What I'm taking forward: at some point you have to go to the garden.

Access and Context

Broader reflections on the studio

What This Studio Changed

I came into this subject thinking about accessibility as something you add to work after you've made it — captions, alt text, ramps. I'm leaving it understanding access as a design method that changes what you make, not just how you deliver it.

The most important shift was understanding that access and creative intention aren't separate concerns. Papalia gave me the language for it, Mingus gave me the relational model, and Hamraie gave me the uncomfortable edge case where those things come into conflict. The iOS problem in Annie's project is where all three converge: I was trying to design for everyone, which meant I couldn't fully design for the people who needed it most. That's not a failure I've resolved. It's a tension I'm carrying into future work.

Fayen d'Evie and Vibrational Poetics

The class example closest to Annie's project was Fayen d'Evie and Benjamin Hancock's vibrational poetics practice — site-specific, multisensory, Australian work demonstrating intersensory publishing operating simultaneously as access practice and as art. This was the precedent that made me confident the Annie concept was valid.

Access Intimacy in Practice

I was skeptical throughout the semester that you could design for access intimacy without it becoming performative. The Sylvia recording is the moment where that theory met practice. I didn't engineer it. I asked someone in my community for something real, and she gave me more than I expected. That's what Mingus is describing. It can't be designed for — but work can create the conditions for it to happen.

Crip Authorship — Questions I Haven't Resolved

Who gets to author work about disability? I'm making a work about Alzheimer's from outside that experience. My connection is personal — my grandmother — but personal isn't lived. I don't think that question has a clean resolution. What I believe is that it needs to stay active in the work rather than be answered away.

A3: Progressive Web App (HTML/CSS/JS), rebuilt on Leaflet/OSM after Mapbox token exposure. Audio recording — Stop 2 (The Gazebo), performed by Sylvia. 3D model of NFC checkpoint puck (qr_puck__UMA_.stl), 3D printed. Puck specification diagram.
